name: John Wayne Sweep
description: Master the John Wayne Sweep from Butterfly Hook Control. High-reward reversal to Mount using two-on-one sleeve control, a pistol grip break, and hook elevation.
summary: The John Wayne Sweep is a butterfly-hook-control reversal that uses two-on-one sleeve control and a signature pistol-grip break to strip the opponent's posting hand, then elevates on the hooks to dump them directly into Mount.
overview:
The John Wayne Sweep is a high-reward reversal from butterfly hook control that uses two-on-one sleeve control and a signature pistol-grip break to strip the opponent's base before elevating them over the butterfly hooks directly into mount. Named for the characteristic pistol-shooting motion of the grip break, it blends classic butterfly elevation mechanics with isolating grip-fighting on a single arm, exploiting the moment an opponent posts a hand or drives forward to defend the hooks.

The sweep operates on a three-phase mechanical sequence: first, a two-on-one grip on the lead sleeve eliminates one posting arm and pulls it across the opponent's centerline to create a rotational axis; second, the pistol grip break removes the remaining posted hand; third, coordinated hook elevation and angular rotation complete the reversal. Because the finish lands directly in mount rather than a scramble, it is one of the highest-reward attacks available from a seated butterfly position.

This sweep is especially effective in the gi, where sleeve grips provide leverage, though no-gi variations exist using wrist and tricep control. It integrates naturally into a broader butterfly guard attack system, chaining with arm drags, basic butterfly sweeps, X-guard entries, and kimura attacks depending on the opponent's defensive reaction. Competition practitioners value it for its direct path to a four-point mount position.

attacker.name: John Wayne Sweep Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute the John Wayne Sweep in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters.
attacker.overview: The John Wayne Sweep is a high-reward butterfly hook control attack that capitalizes on an opponent's forward pressure and poor base management. Named for the pistol-shooting motion used during the grip break, it combines active butterfly hook elevation with creative grip fighting on a single isolated arm. By establishing two-on-one sleeve control, creating an angle with your hips, and driving the butterfly hooks upward, you off-balance the opponent and rotate them directly into mount. The sweep is particularly effective in the gi where sleeve grips provide leverage, though no-gi variations exist using wrist and tricep control.
key_principles: Establish two-on-one sleeve control and active butterfly hooks before initiating sweep momentum
Create angular positioning to break the opponent's base structure from butterfly hook control
Use the butterfly hooks and hip elevation to lift the opponent while controlling the upper body
Time the sweep with the opponent's forward pressure or posting attempt
Maintain tight connection throughout the rotation to prevent scrambles
Follow through completely to secure mount rather than settling for a top scramble
Break the opponent's posted hand using the signature 'pistol' motion when needed
setup_requirements: Butterfly hook control established with both insteps inside the opponent's thighs
Two-on-one grip on the lead sleeve (gi) or wrist and tricep (no-gi)
Opponent applying forward pressure or posting a hand to defend the hooks
Your hips mobile and elevated, ready to create an angle from the seated position
Upright posture maintained with the sleeve control providing the steering connection
Sufficient space to rotate without hitting obstacles or mat boundaries

execution_steps.description: From butterfly hook control, sit up onto your hip and secure a two-on-one grip on the opponent's lead sleeve, one hand on the wrist and the other on the tricep or elbow. Pull this arm across your centerline to break their posting base. In no-gi, grip the wrist and tricep firmly to create the same isolation.

Ensure both insteps are hooked inside the opponent's thighs with constant upward elevation tension. Keep your knees live so the hooks can lift, and angle your hips toward the controlled-sleeve side to maximize leverage for the coming rotation.

While maintaining sleeve control, angle your body approximately 45 degrees toward the controlled-sleeve side. This off-balances the opponent and positions your body for the rotational sweep. Your head should move toward the outside of their controlled arm as you come up onto your hip.

If the opponent posts their free hand on the mat, perform the signature 'John Wayne' motion by forming a pistol shape with your free hand and breaking their posted grip by striking or pushing it away. This removes their primary base point and commits them to the sweep.

execution_steps.action: Elevate on the hooks and rotate
execution_steps.description: Explosively extend your butterfly hooks to elevate the opponent's hips while pulling strongly on the controlled sleeve. Use one hook as the lifting fulcrum and the other to drive the rotation, spiraling them over a diagonal axis. Keep tight sleeve tension to invert their base completely as you rotate underneath.

As the opponent rotates over you, keep pulling the controlled arm and use your legs to guide them past your hips. Release the butterfly hooks at the right moment and immediately climb to mount by bringing your knees up their sides as they land on their back.

Once on top, quickly establish mount control by distributing your weight properly, getting your knees high into their armpits, and maintaining upper body control. Keep the controlled arm trapped if possible to prevent an immediate escape attempt.

common_counters.counter: Opponent withdraws their hips and creates distance when they feel the angle developing
common_counters.your_response: Follow their backward movement into an X-guard or single-leg-X entry, or re-pummel the hooks and re-establish the two-on-one to reset butterfly hook control

common_counters.counter: Opponent establishes a strong crossface and drives forward with shoulder pressure to flatten you
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward pressure to elevate into the sweep, or drop under their weight into deep half guard and re-attack from there

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts the free hand strongly and distributes weight over it to prevent the pistol break
common_counters.your_response: Attack the posted arm with a kimura grip instead of breaking it, forcing them to defend the submission while you transition to a different sweep or back take

common_counters.counter: Opponent sprawls and flattens their body weight down onto you to kill the elevation
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the dying sweep, re-pummel to butterfly hooks or insert a knee shield to recreate space, or drop to deep half guard rather than fighting from flat

common_errors.error: Attempting the sweep without establishing proper sleeve control first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily posts their free arm and prevents the sweep, potentially passing your guard during the failed attempt
common_errors.correction: Always secure a dominant two-on-one grip before initiating any angular movement or elevation. The sleeve control is the foundation that makes the entire technique work

common_errors.error: Creating the angle too early before the opponent commits forward pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the setup and simply withdraws their hips, nullifying the sweep and creating distance
common_errors.correction: Wait for the opponent to apply forward pressure or post before creating your angle. Time the sweep with their commitment to moving forward

common_errors.error: Failing to break the posted hand and attempting the sweep anyway
common_errors.consequence: Opponent maintains their base through the posted arm, resulting in an incomplete sweep or getting stuck in a scramble
common_errors.correction: Execute the pistol grip break decisively when the opponent posts. If unable to break it, immediately attack with a kimura or transition to a different technique

common_errors.error: Extending the butterfly hooks too early without rotational momentum
common_errors.consequence: You lift the opponent slightly but they land back in base, wasting energy and telegraphing future attempts
common_errors.correction: Coordinate hook extension with the angular rotation and sleeve pull simultaneously. All three components must work together as one explosive movement

common_errors.error: Releasing sleeve control during the rotation phase
common_errors.consequence: Opponent regains posture mid-sweep and recovers their base or counters by taking the top position
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant tension on the controlled sleeve throughout the entire sweep until you have established mount. The grip is your steering wheel

common_errors.error: Not following through to mount and stopping in a scramble
common_errors.consequence: Missing the opportunity to secure a dominant position and allowing the opponent to defend or re-guard
common_errors.correction: Commit fully to the sweep by continuing the rotational momentum and immediately bringing your knees up to establish mount as the opponent lands

training_progressions.focus: Establishing and maintaining two-on-one sleeve control from butterfly guard
training_progressions.description: Partner offers a static butterfly guard position. Practice securing two-on-one grips on the sleeve, breaking the centerline, and creating angular positioning. Focus on grip strength and control rather than completing sweeps. Drill the pistol grip break motion repetitively.

training_progressions.focus: Synchronizing the sleeve pull, hook extension, and rotation
training_progressions.description: Partner allows the sweep to develop slowly. Practice coordinating all three components of the sweep with emphasis on timing and technique. Partner maintains light base to allow repetitions while providing feedback on technique gaps. Complete 10-15 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Recognizing setup opportunities during live movement
training_progressions.description: Start from standing and pull guard to butterfly, immediately looking for the John Wayne Sweep opportunity. Partner applies forward pressure naturally. Practice reading their weight distribution and timing your angle creation with their commitment. Focus on reactive execution.

training_progressions.focus: Adapting to common counters and maintaining offensive initiative
training_progressions.description: Partner actively defends the sweep using distance creation, underhooks, or strong posts. Practice recognizing when the sweep is not available and transitioning smoothly to alternatives like X-guard, deep half guard, or kimura. Maintain offensive pressure throughout.

training_progressions.focus: Executing the technique under full resistance with consequences
training_progressions.description: Live rolling with the specific goal of hitting the John Wayne Sweep from butterfly guard. Partner uses full defensive tactics and counter-passing attempts. Practice chaining the technique with other butterfly attacks and maintaining composure under pressure.

training_progressions.focus: Seamless integration with the complete butterfly guard system
training_progressions.description: Free rolling with emphasis on using the John Wayne Sweep as part of a larger guard retention and sweeping system. Combine with arm drags, back takes, and submission threats. Focus on reading the opponent's defensive patterns and selecting the optimal technique.

flashcards.question: Why is establishing two-on-one sleeve control essential before attempting the John Wayne Sweep?
flashcards.answer: Two-on-one sleeve control serves multiple critical functions: it breaks your opponent's ability to post on that side, creates an angle by pulling their arm across their centerline which disrupts their base, provides a steering mechanism to guide them through the sweep, and prevents them from establishing underhooks or grips on that side. Without this control, the opponent can easily post and maintain their base throughout your sweep attempt.

flashcards.question: What is the mechanical purpose of creating a 45-degree angle before executing the sweep?
flashcards.answer: The angular positioning off-balances your opponent by moving their center of gravity outside their base of support. When you angle toward the controlled-sleeve side, you create a rotational axis that your opponent cannot defend by simply widening their base. This angle also positions your body optimally to rotate underneath theirs during the sweep while maintaining leverage through the butterfly hooks. The angle transforms a linear lifting motion into a circular sweeping motion with far greater mechanical efficiency.

flashcards.question: Your opponent successfully withdraws their hips backward as you create your angle - how should you adjust?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent withdraws their hips, immediately follow their backward momentum by transitioning to X-guard or single leg X-guard. Keep your top butterfly hook active while inserting your bottom hook behind their knee as they move back. Alternatively, transition to seated guard with ankle pick entries or follow them to standing and attack with wrestling-based takedowns. The key is recognizing that their backward movement creates different opportunities rather than fighting against it.

flashcards.question: What biomechanical principles make the butterfly hooks effective during the elevation phase of this sweep?
flashcards.answer: The butterfly hooks create leverage by positioning your feet under your opponent's center of gravity at their hip and thigh junction. When you extend your legs, you create a first-class lever where your hips are the fulcrum, your extending legs are the effort arm, and your opponent's upper body is the resistance arm. The close proximity of your hips to theirs maximizes mechanical advantage. The hooks also prevent lateral escape by controlling the inside thigh position, forcing the opponent's weight to rotate over you rather than stepping out.

flashcards.question: When should you release your butterfly hooks during the sweep rotation?
flashcards.answer: Release your butterfly hooks at the moment your opponent's hips pass the vertical plane above you and their weight begins falling to the opposite side. Releasing too early results in incomplete rotation and scrambles. Releasing too late causes your legs to become trapped underneath them, preventing you from establishing mount. The optimal timing is when you feel their weight commit past the tipping point, typically when their back is facing the ceiling and their momentum is irreversible.

flashcards.question: How does the John Wayne Sweep integrate with other butterfly guard attacks to create a systematic approach?
flashcards.answer: The John Wayne Sweep works synergistically with arm drags, basic butterfly sweeps, and X-guard entries. If the opponent defends the pistol break, you attack kimura. If they withdraw their hips, you enter X-guard. If they drive forward with an underhook, you execute a basic butterfly sweep to that side. If they remain neutral, you arm drag to a back take. This creates a decision tree where every defensive reaction opens a different offensive opportunity, embodying the dilemma creation that defines effective guard systems.

flashcards.question: Your opponent posts their free hand firmly on the mat and you cannot break it with the pistol motion - what are your options?
flashcards.answer: When the pistol grip break fails, immediately transition to attacking the posted arm with a kimura grip by circling your free hand under their wrist and clasping your own wrist. This forces them either to defend the submission by pulling their arm back, which removes their base and allows the sweep, or to remain posted and risk the kimura finish. You can also use the moment they defend the kimura to regrip and attempt the sweep from a different angle, or transition to an arm drag on that posted arm to access the back.

flashcards.question: What is the most critical hip movement in the John Wayne Sweep and why does it differ from a standard butterfly sweep?
flashcards.answer: The critical hip movement is the angular rotation toward the controlled-sleeve side, creating approximately 45 degrees of offset before elevation. Unlike a standard butterfly sweep which uses primarily vertical elevation with lateral tilting, the John Wayne Sweep emphasizes rotational movement that spirals the opponent over a diagonal axis. Your hips must stay connected to the opponent throughout this rotation. This angular approach is harder to defend because it attacks the opponent's base on a vector they cannot counter by simply widening their knees.

flashcards.question: What grip requirements distinguish the John Wayne Sweep from the basic butterfly sweep?
flashcards.answer: The John Wayne Sweep requires a dominant two-on-one grip on the opponent's lead sleeve or arm, with one hand controlling the wrist and the other at the elbow or tricep. This differs from the basic butterfly sweep which typically uses an underhook on one side and collar or head control on the other. The two-on-one configuration is essential because it isolates one arm completely, creating a structural imbalance that the pistol grip break then exploits. The free hand must also be available for the signature pistol motion, which is unique to this sweep.

flashcards.question: Your opponent sprawls their legs back and flattens their weight down as you begin the angle - what is the correct response?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent sprawls and flattens, your butterfly hooks lose their mechanical advantage because the angle of elevation becomes ineffective against a flat opponent. The correct response is to immediately abandon the sweep rather than burning energy against a nullified position. Transition to closed guard by locking your legs around their waist before they can advance, or reset to seated butterfly guard by framing on their shoulders and scooting your hips back. Forcing the sweep against a sprawled opponent wastes energy and exposes you to guard passing.

attacker.safety_considerations: The John Wayne Sweep is generally a low-risk technique for both practitioners when executed properly. The primary safety concern is ensuring sufficient mat space for the rotation, as the sweep involves rotating the opponent over your body with momentum. Practice initially on soft surfaces and ensure no obstacles are nearby. Partners should be aware of the incoming sweep to avoid reflexively posting with their arm at dangerous angles, which can cause wrist or shoulder injuries. When drilling, the bottom practitioner should control the speed of rotation initially to prevent unexpected impacts. Advanced practitioners should be mindful of their partner's flexibility limitations when pulling the controlled arm across the centerline, as excessive force can strain the shoulder. In competition settings, be aware of mat boundaries to avoid rotating your opponent off the mat.

defender.name: John Wayne Sweep Defender
defender.description: How to defend against the John Wayne Sweep in BJJ. Recognition cues, defensive options, and escape strategies.
defender.overview:
Defending the John Wayne Sweep requires understanding its three-phase execution sequence and intercepting at the earliest possible stage. The sweep depends on a chain of prerequisites: two-on-one sleeve control, angular positioning, the pistol grip break, and coordinated hook elevation. Each phase presents a distinct defensive window, and the earlier you intervene, the higher your success rate. Once the rotation begins with full momentum, defensive options narrow dramatically.

From the top position against active butterfly hooks, your primary defensive objective is denying the two-on-one grip from isolating your arm across your centerline while keeping your weight back and off the hooks. If the grip is established, your secondary objective becomes maintaining a strong posting base while working to recover the controlled arm. The sweep becomes nearly unstoppable once both your posting base and arm control are compromised, so defensive urgency escalates with each phase the attacker completes.

Effective defense integrates grip fighting, base management, and tactical weight distribution. Keeping your weight back off the hooks and denying the two-on-one neutralizes the setup. If the attacker achieves the angle, strong posting combined with driving your weight forward and down can nullify the elevation. Skilled defenders also use the attacker's commitment against them by timing guard passes during the rotation attempt, capitalizing on the momentary vulnerability created when the bottom player fully commits to the sweep.
key_principles: Deny the two-on-one grip by keeping your elbows tight and grip-fighting actively from the top
Keep your weight back and off the butterfly hooks to deny their elevation leverage
Maintain at least one strong posting point at all times to resist the rotational sweep
Keep your elbows tight to your torso to prevent arm isolation across your centerline
Recognize the pistol grip break motion and immediately redistribute weight to maintain base
Use the attacker's commitment against them by timing counter-passes during full sweep attempts
When the hooks elevate, drive your hips forward and down to flatten their angle
recognition_cues: Opponent secures a two-on-one grip on your lead sleeve, pulling your arm across their body toward their opposite hip
Opponent's body angles approximately 45 degrees to the sleeve-control side while keeping active butterfly hooks inside your thighs
Opponent's free hand forms a pistol shape and moves toward your posted hand on the mat, signaling the signature grip break
You feel simultaneous upward hook elevation and lateral pulling on your controlled arm creating a rotational force vector
Opponent's head drops below your chest level and moves to the outside of your controlled arm as they come up strongly onto their hip

defensive_options.action: Strip the two-on-one grip by circling your controlled elbow back toward your hip and pulling your wrist free with a strong circular motion
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel the opponent establishing two-on-one control on your sleeve, before they can create an angle. This is the highest-percentage defense because it stops the sweep at its foundation.
defensive_options.if_successful: Returns to a neutral top position with the opponent unable to execute the sweep, allowing you to re-establish base and passing grips
defensive_options.risk: If the grip strip fails, you may overextend your arm and give the opponent a deeper angle for the sweep

defensive_options.action: Drop your weight back and off the hooks while widening your base and posting to kill the elevation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the opponent creating angular positioning and loading your weight onto the hooks. Best used before the pistol grip break occurs.
defensive_options.if_successful: Removes your weight from the hooks and kills the elevation angle, resetting to a dominant top position where you can work your passing game
defensive_options.risk: Dropping weight back too far can let the opponent disengage and re-pummel for an arm drag to the back

defensive_options.action: Drive your hips forward and down into the opponent to flatten their angle and pin the hooks, then counter-pass
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent has established the angle but committed fully to the rotation. Use their momentary guard opening to pass.
defensive_options.if_successful: Flattens the opponent and opens a smash pass or over-under pass while their legs are occupied with elevation rather than retention
defensive_options.risk: If the opponent still has the two-on-one secured, driving forward can fuel their sweep instead of stopping it

defensive_options.action: Post the free hand wide with a slightly bent arm and redistribute weight over the post when you feel the pistol break attempt
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent attempts the signature pistol grip break on your posted hand. Stiffen the post slightly, widen your base, and shift your center of gravity over it.
defensive_options.if_successful: Maintains your base structure despite the grip break attempt, forcing the opponent to abandon the sweep or transition to a different attack
defensive_options.risk: Posting with a straight arm creates vulnerability to a kimura attack if the opponent switches from grip break to submission

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the two-on-one grip early by circling your elbow back to your hip, then re-establish base and passing posture. Alternatively, drop your weight back off the hooks to nullify the elevation and settle into a half guard pass.

Time a counter-pass during the opponent's sweep commitment. When they fully commit to the rotation, their butterfly structure is momentarily weakened. Drive forward through their legs with a smash pass or over-under pass, flattening their guard and advancing toward side control.

common_errors.error: Allowing the two-on-one grip to establish without immediately contesting it through active grip fighting
common_errors.consequence: Once the two-on-one is secured, your arm is isolated across the opponent's centerline, removing one posting option and making the sweep significantly easier to execute
common_errors.correction: Fight grips immediately and continuously. The moment you feel the opponent grabbing your sleeve with both hands, circle your elbow back toward your hip and pull your wrist free. Prevent the grip from settling by keeping your arms active.

common_errors.error: Leaning forward and loading your weight onto the hooks when you feel off-balanced by the grip pull
common_errors.consequence: Your forward momentum becomes the primary energy source for the sweep, making elevation effortless for the attacker and the rotation nearly unstoppable
common_errors.correction: When you feel the pull from the two-on-one grip, resist the instinct to drive your weight onto the hooks. Instead, sit your weight back, widen your base, and work to recover the controlled arm from a balanced posture.

common_errors.error: Posting with a straight, locked-out arm when the opponent attempts the pistol grip break
common_errors.consequence: Creates a rigid lever that the pistol motion can easily break, and exposes the arm to a kimura attack if the opponent switches strategy
common_errors.correction: Post with a slightly bent arm and distribute weight broadly rather than concentrating it on a single point. Keep your elbow slightly bent and your hand wide, ready to adjust the post dynamically.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the sweep direction during rotation instead of facing into it
common_errors.consequence: Exposes your back to a potential back take if the sweep partially succeeds, converting a recovery situation into an even worse positional crisis
common_errors.correction: Always face toward the direction of the sweep rotation. If you feel the rotation beginning, turn into it and work to establish or maintain the top position.

common_errors.error: Attempting to stand up while the two-on-one grip is still fully secured on your arm
common_errors.consequence: Standing with a compromised arm gives the opponent a direct entry to X-guard or single leg X-guard, trading one bad position for another
common_errors.correction: Strip or at least partially compromise the two-on-one grip before standing. If you must stand with the grip intact, immediately circle the controlled arm free as you create distance.

flashcards.question: What is the single most important defensive action against the John Wayne Sweep and at what stage should it occur?
flashcards.answer: The most important defensive action is stripping the two-on-one grip on your sleeve before the attacker can establish angular positioning. This should occur immediately when you feel both of the opponent's hands securing your sleeve or wrist. The two-on-one grip is the foundation of the entire sweep; without it, the attacker cannot isolate your arm, create the rotational axis, or execute the pistol grip break. Every subsequent defensive option has a lower success rate than preventing this initial grip.

flashcards.question: Why is keeping your weight back off the hooks a more effective defense than driving forward when you feel the sweep developing?
flashcards.answer: Keeping your weight back removes your center of gravity from the butterfly hooks' elevation range, neutralizing the mechanical advantage the hooks provide. Driving your weight forward onto the hooks is counterproductive because the John Wayne Sweep specifically exploits forward pressure as the energy source for elevation and rotation. By keeping your weight off the hooks and posting wide, you deny the sweep its required mechanical input while making the two-on-one grip less effective as a steering mechanism.

flashcards.question: You feel the opponent's free hand forming the pistol shape and moving toward your posted hand - what is your immediate response?
flashcards.answer: Immediately shift your weight to widen your base and strengthen the posting arm. Bend your elbow slightly to create a more resilient post that cannot be easily broken by the pistol strike. Simultaneously begin circling your controlled arm free from the two-on-one grip, using the momentary distraction of the pistol attempt. If the pistol break connects, have a secondary post ready, so prepare to post with your head or opposite hand to maintain base while recovering structure.

flashcards.question: How can you use the attacker's full commitment to the sweep rotation as a counter-passing opportunity?
flashcards.answer: When the attacker fully commits to the rotation by extending the hooks and pulling strongly on your arm, their guard structure is temporarily compromised because both legs are occupied with elevation rather than retention. If you can maintain base through the initial rotation by posting strongly, you can immediately drive forward through their opened guard with a smash pass, over-under pass, or body lock pass. The key timing window is when the sweep fails but the attacker's legs have not yet recovered to a defensive configuration.

flashcards.question: What recognition cues distinguish a John Wayne Sweep setup from a standard butterfly sweep setup?
flashcards.answer: The defining cue is the two-on-one grip configuration on a single arm, which differs from the standard butterfly sweep's typical underhook plus collar or head control. Additionally, the John Wayne Sweep involves a more pronounced angular body rotation to approximately 45 degrees before elevation, whereas the standard butterfly sweep attacks more laterally. The signature pistol grip break motion is unique to this sweep. If you feel both of the opponent's hands on one of your arms combined with angular hip movement, you are facing a John Wayne Sweep rather than a standard butterfly sweep.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying John Wayne Sweep setups and preventing the two-on-one grip
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly works through the John Wayne Sweep setup phases while you practice recognizing each stage. Focus exclusively on stripping the two-on-one grip using elbow circles and wrist extraction. No passing or countering yet - just recognition and grip prevention at various stages of the setup.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining posting structure during active sweep attempts
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes the full John Wayne Sweep setup including the two-on-one grip and angle. Practice maintaining base through strong posting, weight distribution, and keeping your weight off the hooks as the partner attempts the full sweep with increasing intensity. Focus on staying balanced through the rotation attempt rather than stripping grips.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Counter-Passing and Tactical Weight Movement
training_progressions.focus: Converting defensive survival into offensive passing opportunities
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the full John Wayne Sweep against your active defense. Practice keeping your weight off the hooks, posting strongly, and timing counter-passes when the sweep attempt fails. Work on reading which defensive response is appropriate based on the stage of the sweep setup.

training_progressions.focus: Defending against the John Wayne Sweep under full resistance
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting against butterfly hooks with the partner specifically hunting for the John Wayne Sweep. Defend with your full technical repertoire including grip fighting, weight management, posting, and counter-passing. Partner chains the sweep with other butterfly attacks to simulate realistic offensive pressure and test defensive adaptability.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Executed with wrist and tricep control instead of sleeve grips. Requires a stronger connection and faster execution due to reduced friction. Often combined with a Russian tie control on the lead arm.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In no-gi grappling or MMA contexts where gi grips are unavailable. Particularly effective when the opponent reaches for underhooks aggressively.

variants_and_adaptations.description: If the opponent posts strongly and prevents mount, maintain the sleeve control and use the momentum to take the back instead. Insert your bottom hook as they rotate and establish seat belt control.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent successfully posts during the sweep but you have already committed to the rotation. Allows you to salvage an offensive position rather than returning to guard.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Control both sleeves instead of using the pistol break, pulling both arms across the centerline simultaneously. Creates even more off-balancing but requires exceptional grip strength.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against smaller opponents or those with weaker grips. Also effective when the opponent keeps both hands high and available for control.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Execute the same two-on-one and pistol-break sequence from half guard, using the trapped-leg half-guard hook for elevation instead of double butterfly hooks. The upper-body mechanics transfer directly while the lower-body engine changes to the half-guard hook.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you are in half guard rather than seated butterfly. The grip fighting and pistol break are identical; only the leg used for elevation changes.

position_integration: The John Wayne Sweep is a high-reward attack within the butterfly hook control system and an extension of classic butterfly elevation mechanics. It integrates with the fundamental butterfly philosophy of using active hooks to off-balance the opponent while isolating an arm to remove a posting base. The technique serves as a bridge between basic butterfly sweeps and more dynamic attacks like arm-drag back takes and X-guard entries, since the grip controls and hook elevation are transferable. As part of a complete butterfly attack system, the John Wayne Sweep provides a direct threat to mount, one of the most dominant positions in BJJ, making it particularly valuable in competition settings where point-scoring is crucial.
